strengths: Novel geometric characterization of feasible classifiers under sufficiency, with elegant connection to fractional knapsack and piecewise hyperbolic boundary structure
Addresses practically important gap in prior work by handling finite-valued score distributions rather than requiring continuity and full support
Rigorous mathematical framework with complete proofs; properly handles intersection of subgroup-feasible regions and provides clear algorithmic procedures
General optimization framework accommodates arbitrary loss functions and multiple objectives (loss minimization, deviation from separation), not limited to specific problems
Well-written presentation with clear mathematical exposition and effective visualizations; honest treatment of limitations including degenerate cases
Exact solution rather than approximation; methodologically sound with thorough treatment of edge cases
weaknesses: Severely limited empirical validation: single COMPAS dataset with no baseline comparisons, marginal accuracy improvement (0.677 vs 0.681), and no ablation studies or sensitivity analysis

Strong input assumption requiring group-calibrated scores, but paper provides no guidance on obtaining such scores in practice or handling approximate calibration; COMPAS example uses 20% of data just for calibration

Practical impact unclear—COMPAS results show different group-specific thresholds which practitioners likely already apply; no demonstration that exact optimal solution substantially outperforms simpler heuristics

Scope limited to binary classification and sufficiency constraint; generalization to multiclass or other fairness notions not discussed; known incompatibility with separation is acknowledged but not deeply explored
Computational complexity of Algorithm 1 not explicitly stated; COMPAS example shows the two optimization objectives often coincide without explanation of when/why they diverge
Missing technical details on numerical stability, finite-sample verification of group-calibration, and detailed baseline comparisons that would establish practical relevance

strengths: Novel geometric characterization of feasible (PPV, FOR) pairs under sufficiency with elegant theoretical framework connecting to fractional knapsack optimization
Practical post-processing algorithm (Algorithm 1) that works with finite-valued, group-calibrated scores without requiring access to raw features or model retraining
Rigorous mathematical treatment including complete proofs, handling of degenerate cases (Appendix D), and robustness analysis for approximate calibration (Appendix J)
Well-motivated problem highlighting a genuine gap in the fairness literature: sufficiency is not preserved under post-processing, unlike independence and separation
Principled extension to multi-objective optimization (loss minimization and deviation from separation) within the same geometric framework
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core observation that thresholding violates sufficiency is known from prior work (Chouldechova 2017, Canetti et al. 2019); main contribution is solving for finite-valued case only

Restrictive assumptions significantly limit scope: group-calibration requirement is demanding in practice, and approximate calibration in ACS experiment shows ~0.48% PPV gap violations (not negligible)

Fundamental scalability limitation acknowledged by authors: the approach fails for multiple protected groups as feasible region intersection becomes empty more frequently—severely limits real-world applicability
Weak empirical validation: no comparison with Baumann et al. (2022) or Canetti et al. (2019); only unconstrained Bayes baselines; ACS shows modest accuracy difference (0.23 percentage points)

Incomplete practical guidance: no principled method for choosing between loss minimization vs. deviation-from-separation objectives; limited discussion of when sufficiency is appropriate vs. other fairness notions
Binary classification only and finite-valued scores assumption, while practical, limits theoretical generality and applicability to continuous or multiclass settings
Missing important details: computational complexity not analyzed; no runtime comparisons; limited ablation studies; FICO/COMPAS experiments use aggregate statistics rather than raw data

strengths: Technically sound with rigorous mathematical development; elegant use of fractional knapsack framework (Theorem 3.3) and precise characterization of feasible region boundaries (Theorem 3.4)
Addresses genuine practical problem: demonstrates that perfectly calibrated scores violate sufficiency after thresholding, relevant to systems like COMPAS and FICO
Novel geometric framework using star-convexity provides new insights into fairness-accuracy trade-offs and enables practical algorithms for exact optimization
Algorithm 1 is concrete, implementable, and naturally accommodates multiple objectives (loss minimization, separation-deviation minimization)
Strong experimental validation: ACS Income experiment with 100 train/test splits and cross-validated calibration is convincing; consistent small sufficiency violations across domains
Comprehensive treatment of important details: degenerate cases (Appendix D), calibration robustness analysis (Appendix J), and separation-deviation minimization (Section 6)
Clear pedagogical presentation progressing logically from unconstrained to multi-group constrained settings with effective geometric visualizations
weaknesses: Limited scope reduces broader impact: restriction to finite scores prevents application to continuous systems; binary-group focus leaves k>2 case for future work; strong group-calibration assumption is required for exact guarantees

Missing critical baseline comparisons: no empirical comparison with Baumann et al. (2022) which also achieves sufficiency; only unconstrained baselines limits claims about practical advantage of avoiding continuity assumptions

Sufficiency is specialized fairness notion: paper acknowledges incompatibility with separation but provides limited guidance on when practitioners should prefer sufficiency over independence/separation; no empirical studies of stakeholder preferences

Incomplete theoretical analysis: no characterization of when C⁰ ∩ C¹ is empty/small in practice; linear robustness bound (2ε) to calibration error is loose compared to empirical observations; why observed violations are smaller lacks theoretical explanation

Experimental limitations weaken claims: FICO/COMPAS use pre-existing aggregate statistics without train-test splits; no systematic comparison of accuracy loss under sufficiency vs. natural accuracy-fairness trade-offs for other fairness notions; ACS Income treats ~calibrated scores as perfectly calibrated despite non-trivial violations (4.8×10⁻³ PPV gap)

Technical presentation gaps: choice of total variation divergence for Δ_sep (Equation 14) lacks justification; degenerate case handling (Appendix D) appears somewhat ad-hoc; mixture construction implementation and practical acceptance of randomized rules underexplored
Reproducibility gaps: quantitative experimental details scattered across appendices; out-of-fold calibration procedure not fully specified in main algorithmic presentation
